concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.

A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Control of the centre
concepts.wording: Control of the centre: influence over the four central squares, whether by occupying them with pawns or attacking them from a distance with pieces. Occupation gives space; control without commitment avoids giving a target.
cautions: Occupying the centre is not always right — an unsupported pawn centre is a target, which is the hypermodern case.
Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.

concept.wording: A discovered attack: two attacks for one move — whatever the moving piece does, and whatever the piece behind it now hits. The moving piece is comparatively free, because the opponent has to deal with the revealed threat.
cautions: A discovery is worthless if the unmasked line hits nothing of value.
In a discovered check the moving piece may stand en prise with impunity — normal safety reasoning does not apply to it.

concept.name: Passed pawn
concept.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concept.name: Restraint
concept.wording: Restraint: preventing enemy pawns and pieces from advancing, as progress in its own right. It is the first stage of Nimzowitsch's formula — first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.
cautions: Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.

It wins the pawn. A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.

concept.name: Pawn break
concept.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

concept.name: Hanging piece
concept.why: It leaves the rook on e8 hanging — it can simply be taken.
concept.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.
